item.title: Bitcoin follows the flows and today that flow is "risk-off" and selling.
item.description:
The swings in bitcoin continue. The price is currently down nearly $3,000, trading near $81,000 after reaching a low of $80,836. Today’s high reached $84,294, below yesterday’s high at $84,774.

Both highs stalled ahead of the next key upside swing level at $85,578. Buyers had their shot to extend the recovery, but they could not reach that hurdle. Today, sellers have taken back control.

Bitcoin follows the risk-off flows

The move lower has been helped by risk-off sentiment across the equity markets:

  • Nasdaq Composite: Down 2.56%.

  • Nasdaq 100: Down 2.82%.

Bitcoin is following the equity market’s lead—at least today. When investors are reducing risk, bitcoin can get caught in the same selling flow. That is what the price action is showing in this session.

The lower swing area is back in play

Technically, today’s decline has taken the price into a lower swing area between $80,100 and $81,183. That area has helped define the bottom of bitcoin’s consolidation range since September 18. Monday’s low at $80,595 also stalled within that zone.

That gives traders a clear area to watch. Buyers need to defend support and push the price back above $81,183 to begin easing the immediate downside pressure. Holding support would give them a foothold, but they would still need to build on it.

For sellers, the next step is a sustained break below the lower boundary. Call $80,000 the line in the sand. Get below and stay below, and the door opens for more downside momentum.

What comes next on a break?

Below the consolidation range, the 38.2% retracement of the move higher from the July low comes in at $76,052. That becomes the next major technical target if sellers can establish control below $80,000.

The distinction is important: testing support is one thing. Breaking below it and staying below it is another. Sellers need that next shove to turn another swing within the range into a break out of the range.

In the video above, I take a look at bitcoin’s latest swings, the support being tested, and what buyers and sellers need to do next.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The market now sees a 22% chance the Fed doesn't hike again this year
item.description:
The Fed funds futures marketr now sees a 22% that the Federal Reserve is done hiking rates for this year.

That's a big swing to where we were after the CPI report, which is the most-revelant number the Fed should be thinking about next week. Instead, the market is focused on how the FOMC will react to the stock market, which is slumping on AI capital raising fears. 

For next week's meeting, the market now sees only a 5% chance of a hike, the lowest this month. For December, it's still at a 78% chance of a hike but no longer a sure thing. January pricing is at 27 basis points, which is barely pricing in a single hike.

Looking further out the curve, the market sees 63.5 bps this year, a far cry from the 80-90 bps priced in earlier this month.

You can also see a major repricing underway in the bond market as 2-year yields are down 18 basis points to 4.64% today. It comes after Meta filed for a new class of shares. The share filingindicates that all three long-term forecasts presented to the Board contemplated raising hundreds of billions of dollars, potentially beginning as early this autumn. Management also viewed an  equity raise as “essential” to anticipated business plans and expects additional near-term capital, including equity.

The fixed income market could be taking a view that AI bonds are now tapped out and capital raising will now fall to equity. That's bad news for share prices and Meta is down 7.5% today but it could also mean less issuance of debt, which could limit crowding out in bonds. The lack of capital could also be causing jitters about the value in the broader AI build out and signal a retrechment in the entire trade.

The problem for the Fed is that a slump in AI capital raises might not be the tonic to curb inflation. The Iran blockade continues and oil prices are up $2.35 to $99.50 today with fuel prices much higher still. That will be plenty of fuel for the hawks and make for a lively debate (and maybe a split vote?) next week.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: The evidence mounts that the US dollar is leveraged to the AI trade
item.description:
Today's price action is another reminder that the underpinnings of the US dollar's rally this year is AI capex spending.

It's an intense risk-off day and yet the US dollar is down on most fronts or close to flat. It just fell into negative territory against the euro on the day despite riots and debt concerns in France. It's also sitting at a one-month low against the Canadian dollar and down 120 pips against the yen.

Some of that is a sharp drop in Treasury yields but in the bigger picture, it's all one big trade: AI.

Right now, the market is questioning where all the money will come from to fund the AI build out and finding a tough time making the math work. The costs are so staggaringly high and it's so crowded that would-be lenders are tapped out and the broader investing public is skeptical of piling into a crowded trade. 

It's now abundantly clear that much of the USD outperformance in the past year has been money flowing towards the US capex buildout and associated equities. If you wanted to invest in AI, the USA was the only real game in town. Now with valuations stretched and some questions about how the frontier models will compete with open source models, the economics of it all are in question. That's leading to a reverse of the same flows that drove the USD higher.

Moreover, the fundamentals don't support the US dollar at current levels in a world that's seeing trading relationships fray and the US stuck in a quagmire in Iran. So even if AI stands still, there's a force of gravity on the US dollar that's negative and needs constant AI dollars to support it. Said differently, it's only a matter of time until the dollar retreats.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US stocks are taking on water. What could steady the ships?
item.description:
The S&P 500, Nasdaq Composite and Nasdaq 100 are under technical pressure. Key support levels could offer a lifeline, but buyers need to prove they can hold them.

The broader US stock indices are trading near their lows for the day. If the indices were ships on the water, they would be taking on water.

Broken moving averages have tilted the technical bias toward the sellers. However, support targets loom below that could help steady the ships. The question is whether buyers can lean against those levels and force a recovery—or whether sellers punch another hole in the hull.

S&P 500: A key support zone comes into view

  • The S&P 500 has fallen below its 100-hour moving average at 7754 and 200-hour moving average at 7714. Those breaks give sellers more control and turn the moving averages into resistance on a recovery.

The next key downside focus is the rising 100-day moving average at 7603, which sits inside a swing area between 7573 and 7617.

That combination makes this an important zone for buyers. Holding it could give them a platform for a bounce. Break below 7573 and stay below, however, and the door opens for further selling momentum.

For now, support is approaching. Buyers still need to show up.

Nasdaq Composite: The broken 100-day moving average defines risk

  • The Nasdaq Composite tested its 200-hour moving average yesterday, but fell sharply at today’s open and broke below its 100-day moving average at 26265.87.

That 100-day moving average now becomes a nearby risk-defining level. Stay below it and sellers retain the technical advantage. Move back above and stay above, and some of the immediate downward pressure would ease.

Without that recovery, the next downside targets are the September low at 25831.74, followed by the 38.2% retracement at 25036.33 and the rising 200-day moving average at 24980.37.

The retracement and 200-day moving average form another important support zone. But the first job for buyers is to reclaim the broken 100-day moving average. Until then, sellers remain in control.

Nasdaq 100: Buyers get a chance against a swing area

  • The Nasdaq 100 gapped below its 100-day moving average at 29589.57 at the open and extended to a session low of 28962.36. That brought the index within about nine points of the upper boundary of a swing area between 28822 and 28953.

This is where buyers have an opportunity to make a stand.

If the index can hold that swing area, a recovery toward the broken 100-day moving average becomes a possibility. Getting back above **29589.57—and staying above—**would give buyers more control from a technical perspective.

Conversely, a break below 28822 would weaken that recovery scenario and expose the 38.2% retracement of the rally from the 2026 low at 28108.

The distinction matters: holding support can start a bounce. Reclaiming the broken moving average would strengthen the case that buyers are taking back control.

Support could steady the ships. The bias remains bearish.

The broader indices are sinking, but each has identifiable support ahead that could help slow the selling.

Support, however, is a place to watch for a response. It is not a guarantee that the decline is over. Buyers need to hold those levels and then reclaim the technical levels broken on the way down.

Until that happens, the bias remains more bearish.

item.title: US treasury excels $26 billion of five-year tips at a high yield of 2.367%
item.description:
The Treasury sold $26 billion of 5-year Treasury Inflation-Protected Securities, or TIPS, with the following results:

  • High yield: 2.367%.
  • WI level at the time of the auction: 2.360%.
  • Tail: 0.7 basis point vs the average of 0.2 basis point.
  • Bid to cover: 2.41X vs the average of 2.52X.
  • Directs: 32.4% vs the average of 23.0%.
  • Indirects: 62.1% vs the average of 67.8%.
  • Dealers: 5.5% vs the average of 9.2%.

Auction grade: C−

A somewhat softer auction overall. The Treasury needed to offer a yield 0.7 basis point above the WI level to get the issue sold, a larger tail than average. Bid to cover was also below average, while indirect bidders (foreign buyers) took a smaller share. The offset was strong direct demand (domestic buyers), which helped leave dealers with just 5.5% of the issue—well below average. So there were some positives underneath the headline, but the tail and softer overall bidding keep the grade below a C-.

What are TIPS, and how do they work?

TIPS provide investors with protection against inflation by adjusting the security’s principal with the Consumer Price Index. When inflation rises, the principal increases. The coupon rate stays fixed, but the dollar interest payments increase as that rate is applied to a larger principal balance. Payments are made every six months. www.treasurydirect.gov

For example, take $1,000 of principal with a hypothetical 2% coupon. If the inflation adjustment lifts that principal to $1,030, the annualized interest payment rises from $20 to $20.60. The coupon rate stays the same; the principal used to calculate the payment changes. www.treasurydirect.gov

Today’s 2.367% auction yield is a real yield, meaning a yield above the security’s CPI inflation adjustment. It is separate from the coupon rate and does not represent the market’s inflation forecast. The difference between a conventional Treasury yield and a TIPS yield of the same maturity provides a measure known as breakeven inflation. www.treasurydirect.gov

At maturity, investors receive the inflation-adjusted principal or the original principal, whichever is greater. That floor protects the original face amount, although it does not necessarily protect any premium paid when purchasing the security.

With the current 5 year yield at 4.7909% what does that tell traders/investors?

Using the 5-year Treasury yield of 4.7909% and today’s TIPS auction yield of 2.367%, the spread is:

4.7909% − 2.367% = 2.4239 percentage points, or 242.39 basis points.

That is an approximate 5-year breakeven inflation rate of 2.42%, assuming the yields are measured at the same time and have comparable maturities.

In plain English, the conventional Treasury pays a higher yield because its payments do not adjust for inflation. The TIPS offers a lower real yield, with CPI inflation adjustments added through its principal. The spread represents the inflation compensation priced into the comparison. TIPS Yield Curve and Inflation Compensation

For an investor holding to maturity, roughly speaking:

  • Average CPI inflation above 2.42%: TIPS would tend to deliver the better return.
  • Average CPI inflation below 2.42%: The conventional Treasury would tend to deliver the better return.
  • Average CPI inflation near 2.42%: Returns would be broadly comparable.

That is an approximation; cash-flow timing and reinvestment also matter.

What does today’s auction tell us? The spread is consistent with investors pricing inflation averaging around the mid-2% area over the next five years. It does not mean inflation will be 2.42% every year, or that this is a precise forecast. Breakevens also reflect inflation-risk compensation and differences in liquidity between conventional Treasuries and TIPS. Tips from TIPS: Update and Discussions

The auction itself was somewhat soft, with a 0.7-basis-point tail. Holding the conventional yield unchanged, that higher TIPS yield would narrow the breakeven spread by 0.7 basis point compared with the pre-auction WI level. But that small auction concession alone does not establish that inflation expectations are falling. We would need the earlier spread, using both yields at matching times, to judge the trend.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: Meta shares fall 7% on huge spending plans
item.description:
• Q3 revenue $64.6B vs $63.3B expected
  • Q4 revenue guide $73–76B vs $73.7B expected
  • Q3 capex $34.9B; free cash flow turned negative
  • 2026 capex $135–145B (floor raised from $130B)
  • $825B in future spending commitments
  • New nonvoting Class C shares through a 2-for-1 split

Meta beat on revenue, beat on guidance, and the stock is still down 7% and that's a troubling sign for everything touching AI. It's also trading below where it did before the rollout of the impressive Muse app. 

Shares are down intraday to $651.61 and were down 7.3% around midday. Meta was off about 3% premarket at $677.50, and the selling has intensified as the session wears on.

w

The ad business isn’t the problem. Revenue rose 26% to $64.6 billion, comfortably ahead of estimates. The Q4 range of $73–76 billion has a $74.5 billion midpoint, above the $73.7 billion consensus, and implies roughly 24% growth. Strip out the lawyers and earnings were even better. GAAP EPS was $3.83 vs $3.56 expected and would have been $7.40 without the legal charge.

If you showed me that revenue line a year ago, I’d have said the stock goes up 10%.

The cash flow line

The problem sits below revenue. Q3 capex hit $34.9 billion, up from $31 billion in Q2 and $19.4 billion a year ago. That pushed free cash flow to negative $2.1 billion, the first negative quarter since 2012.

Total expenses rose 68% y/y to $51.6 billion on infrastructure, third-party AI token costs and a $9.9 billion charge tied to an August agreement with several state attorneys general.

Then there’s the number that will stick. A regulatory filing disclosed about $825 billion in future spending commitments for AI data centers, energy and compute, up from nearly $700 billion in July. That includes $356 billion in leases that haven’t started yet and $455 billion in non-cancelable contracts, with $121 billion due in 2027 alone. The two big buckets went from about $139B to $810B in a year, nearly 6x

Class C is the tell

Financing is increasingly a problem throughout the industry. Meta is creating a nonvoting Class C stock, effective January 19, 2027, and distributing it to all holders as a dividend. It works as a two-for-one split.

Meta says the purpose is to give the company the ability to finance its growth and stay ahead of fierce competition at home and abroad. The market is seeing the new class as a currency that will dilute the company.

The obvious comparison is Alphabet’s 2014 recapitalisation. Class C gives Meta stock to use for employee pay, acquisitions and raising capital. With free cash flow negative, buybacks paused and the AI build-out escalating, it lets management issue stock without diluting Zuckerberg’s voting control.

The bears had already done the arithmetic. Oppenheimer projects about $135 billion in AI- and Muse-driven free cash flow losses through 2028, more than Meta’s roughly $90 billion in cash and securities, and it has flagged the risk of an equity raise and now Meta built the tool to do exactly that. The years of buybacks are going to be unwound quickly.

The bull case hasn’t gone away

The sell side isn’t capitulating. Barclays kept its Overweight rating and raised its target to $880 from $780.

Muse adoption is the main argument. Zuckerberg said more than 10 million people in the US and Canada set up Muse personal agents in the first six weeks, and about a quarter use them daily. He used the word non-stop in the call. Meta also said Reality Labs losses should shrink to around $15 billion in 2027 and move toward profitability after that.

The spending is contractual and front-loaded. Revenue from agents is promising but early.

It’s not just Meta

This is bleeding into the broader AI trade. Tech is the weakest sector, led by Nvidia and AMD, and memory makers Micron and SK Hynix are lower too. Lam Research fell as much as 10% after management flagged supply chain constraints into 2027. The Nasdaq is down 2.3%, and the thinking is that there just isn't enough capital out there to build all the AI that hyperscalers want and they're either going to pay more or scale back plans.

That last point matters more than it gets credit for. A company funding an $825 billion build-out is starting to look at equity markets while the risk-free rate is 5%. Every hurdle rate goes up. The patience for “trust us, the ROI is coming” goes down.

The takeaway is simple. Meta’s core business is as strong as it has ever been. But for the first time in more than a decade, it doesn’t generate enough cash to pay for its ambitions, and management just told you how it plans to fill the gap. Until there are hard returns on Muse, the market will price Meta as a capital-hungry AI infrastructure company rather than a cash-printing ad machine. That’s a lower multiple.

At around $1.65 trillion and 22x trailing earnings, Meta looks cheap on earnings. The market is valuing it on cash flow instead.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: US 10-year yields fall, near 5% level but it's for the wrong reasons
item.description:
The mood in markets isn't good today but there is some good news below the surface for stock markets and gold.

Treasury yields are down 12-14 basis points across the curve as the market gorws increasingly confident that the Fed won't hike rates next week or be overly hawkish. At the 10-year tenure, yields are down 13.5 basis points and nearing the key 5% level.

That's a substantial decline from a high of 5.34% earlies this month, in what was a post-financial crisis high. 

The negative take on the drop in yields is that the tide is going out on the AI trade and investors are seeking safety. That's certainly a consideration strictly in terms of the AI trade. On the other side, there's a large part of the economy that's not AI or particularly vulnerable to AI investment. If the Treasury market is sniffing out a lower-inflation environment, or a less-profilgate Washington, then it would benefit things like home builders.

Not surprisingly, the XHB home builder ETF is up 3% today.

Along those lines, the Russell 2000 jumped earlier this week and even on an ugly day like today in the Nasdaq (-2.4%), it's down just 0.3% today. 

Obviously, the catalysts for a deeper fall in rates could be peace in Ukraine, Iran or Saudi Arabia. Better yet, the combination of all three. 

Technically, the drop below 5% is the key line now. It would actually be worrisome if yields continue to fall at a rapid pace in the abscence of positive news on inflation. 

Here is BMO's take:

The health of corporate credit markets has been in focus as investors remain on guard for emerging signs of stress in the financial system and broader economy. Most immediately relevant, tech bonds have come under pressure, and the rise in credit default swaps on AI-related issuers has been weighing on risk sentiment. While the emerging signs of credit stress have yet to spill over into the broader economy or financial conditions, they have contributed to safe-haven demand for Treasuries, particularly in the long-end.

So it's the right move, but for the wrong reasons.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

item.title: Crude oil buyers remain in control from a technical perspective. What would tilt the bias lower?
item.description:
Middle East risks keep oil supported

Crude oil is moving back toward the $100 level today as Middle East risks give buyers another reason to push prices higher.

In Adam’s post, he outlines the bullish fundamental backdrop for oil: increased military risks involving the US and Israel, a continuing stalemate, and recent Houthi activity in Saudi Arabia adding to the anxiety. A war that was supposed to be quick and easy continues to drag on, keeping concerns about energy supplies firmly in play.

The fundamental story is supportive. The technical price action is helping to confirm that story.

The moving averages help tell the story

Since bottoming on October 6 near $86.93—the 50% midpoint of the move higher from the July 2 low—crude oil has recovered above its 100- and 200-hour moving averages, shown by the blue and green lines on the chart above. Those moving averages have since helped define support and keep the buyers in control.

Initially, the 100-hour moving average provided support. More recently, sellers have managed to push below that faster-moving average, but the breaks have lacked follow-through. The rising 200-hour moving average has held, giving buyers a level to lean against before pushing the price back higher.

That distinction is important for traders. A break below the 100-hour moving average gives sellers an opening. Holding above the 200-hour moving average keeps the buyers in play. To shift control, sellers need to break support and stay below it.

Buyers regain the upper hand today

Today followed that same pattern. The price moved below the 100-hour moving average, held above the 200-hour moving average, and then rebounded back above the 100-hour moving average at $98.23. That recovery puts the buyers back in firmer control as the price works toward $100.

The sellers had their shot below the 100-hour moving average. They could not build on it. Now they need another break—and more follow-through—to threaten the buyers’ control.

What would change the technical picture?

There are three downside levels to watch:

  • $98.23: The 100-hour moving average. A move back below would give sellers some hope, especially if the price stays below.

  • $97.00: The next support level. Breaking below would add to the evidence that sellers are gaining traction.

  • $96.28: The rising 200-hour moving average. A sustained break below would tilt the short-term technical bias back toward the sellers.

Until those levels give way, the sellers have more to prove. Above the 100-hour moving average, buyers remain in control. Below that level but above the 200-hour moving average, buyers remain in play, although their grip becomes less secure.

The trading lesson: Let price confirm the story

The headlines help explain why oil is rising, but the technical levels help traders define risk and recognize when the price action stops supporting the story.

You can have a bullish fundamental view and still need a level that tells you when that view is losing support. For crude oil, the moving averages provide those reference points.

In the video above, I walk through those support levels, explain how the moving averages have guided the move higher, and outline what sellers need to do to take back control.

This article was written by Greg Michalowski at investinglive.com.

item.title: The market can't shake off the stalemate in the Middle East
item.description:
December WTI crude oil is up $2.71 today to $99.84 while brent trades at $112.

The market can't seem to shake off the idea of further escalation before any chance of peace. Republicans are being hammered in the midterms over gasoline prices and an unpopular war but Iran has also dug in and wants concessions before it makes any kind of agreement.

Trump yesterday said the US is not negotiating with Iran.

“No, I think we’re not negotiating," he said.

Later in the day, he repeated a line he's said many times before. “It’ll end very soon. We could leave now, but we want to make sure it lasts for a long time.”

Finally, he said something ominous: 

“We’re gonna have something one way or the other that’ll happen fairly soon. Most people seem to think it’s after the election, and we’re going to see what happens,” he added.

Perhaps that's a hint to Iran making concessions after Republicans are punished at the polls for starting the war? That's the optimistic take but more likely it means that the US will ramp up attacks afterwards and try to break Iran. Along those lines, a report yesterday said that new plans were being drawn up.

Netanyahu was also urging escalation and regime change. He said he discussed the need to topple Iran’s regime with US President Trump on Sunday. Of course  that has to be viewed through the lens of the October 27 elections, where betting odds give him just a 28% chance fo remaining Prime Minister.

On net, the run of headlines lately points to more escalation rather than the short-lived peace hopes from earlier this week. item.title: Trading Education: Gold falls despite lower yields: A lesson in trading what the market gives you
item.description:
Gold typically benefits when Treasury yields and the U.S. dollar move lower. But “typically” is an important word. Those relationships can help frame an expectation. They do not guarantee the next move.

Why do lower yields tend to support gold? Gold pays no interest. When bond yields fall, investors give up less income by owning gold instead of an interest-paying asset. Falling real yields—yields adjusted for inflation—are particularly supportive.

A weaker dollar can also help. Gold is priced in dollars, so a declining greenback makes it less expensive for buyers using other currencies.

When both move lower, gold can get a double tailwind. However, other forces can outweigh those benefits. A decline in the nominal Treasury yield alone also does not tell us what happened to real yields.

Today provides an educational example.

The U.S. 10-year yield is down around 11 basis points to 5.03%. Just last week, it traded at 5.36%. That is a sharp decline and, taken on its own, would normally be considered supportive for gold.

The dollar’s message is less clear. The greenback is lower against the JPY, CHF and CAD, but higher against the EUR, GBP, AUD and NZD. So the double tailwind is not fully in place.

Nevertheless, with yields falling sharply, traders might reasonably have expected gold to find buyers.

Instead, gold is down around $60 and has traded to its lowest level since August.

That is where the technicals become useful. They give traders a way to assess what the market is actually doing and define where that assessment would need to change.

For me, the technical tools help answer three questions:

  • Bias: Are buyers or sellers more in control?

  • Risk: What level would challenge that view?

  • Targets: If momentum continues, where might the price go next?

The hourly chart shows how that framework has played out.

On October 9, gold moved above its 100- and 200-hour moving averages. That shifted the near-term bias in a more bullish direction. Buyers had their shot, and the price moved higher. However, the rally fell short of the October 2 swing high near $4200.

The subsequent decline initially tried to hold support against the moving averages—the blue and green lines—before breaking below them on October 14. That shifted the bias back toward the sellers.

The price then fell to around $4074, stopping short of the October 7 low at $4066.21 before rebounding.

On October 16, buyers pushed back above the moving averages and got another opportunity to take control. Once again, however, the rally stalled near $4200.

Then came another shift.

On October 19, gold fell below the 100- and 200-hour moving averages near $4150. It has remained below those moving averages since.

Today’s rebound reached approximately $4146, stalling just short of the 200-hour moving average, currently at $4147.84. Buyers could not get through that technical hurdle, despite the sharp decline in Treasury yields.

The fundamental backdrop offered a reason to look for buying. The price action had yet to confirm it.

With the moving averages holding as resistance, sellers retained control. The subsequent decline broke below the October low at $4066.21 and reached $4057.52.

That puts $4066.21 in focus. After trading below it, can sellers keep the price below the broken floor? Or will the break fail, allowing buyers to recover above it?

Staying below would keep the downside in play, with the next target area between $4000 and $4018. That zone contains swing lows from July and early August, before gold based and rallied toward its August high of $4698.

A sustained break below $4000 would add to the bearish picture and bring another swing area between $3942 and $3959 into view.

On the upside, reclaiming $4066.21 would be an initial step toward stabilizing the price. However, buyers would ultimately need to get back above—and stay above—the 100- and 200-hour moving averages to shift the near-term bias more convincingly in their favor.

Until then, sellers remain more in control.

The lesson is not that the technicals predict every move. The earlier breaks above the moving averages produced rallies that eventually failed. Their value is that they give traders a framework for responding when the market changes.

Today, lower yields offered a potentially bullish influence. Gold’s failure to reclaim its moving averages kept the technical bias bearish, defined a level against which sellers could manage risk, and left lower targets in play.

Traders do not need to resolve every conflicting fundamental signal before making a decision. They do need to know their bias, where that bias would be challenged, and what comes next if the price keeps moving.

Have an expectation. Then make the market confirm it.

item.title: Netflix, Tesla and Meta earnings put Wall Street's cautious mood back in focus
item.description:
Many bulls are somewhat surprised and trapped in today's pre-market

Wall Street may be sending investors an early warning through the way it is reacting to corporate earnings. After Netflix disappointed investors, Meta and Tesla delivered another revealing development: both stocks initially rose following their October 21 earnings announcements, only to surrender those gains and turn negative ahead of Thursday's U.S. trading session.

The concern is not simply that several popular stocks have declined. It is that investors initially welcomed some encouraging results, but that enthusiasm did not last.

For investors holding these companies, or exposed to them through S&P 500 and Nasdaq-linked funds, this changing reaction to earnings deserves attention.

As Justin Low at investingLive.com pointed out, active traders are navigating a fragile tape as U.S. futures tumble amid mounting scrutiny over the AI rally and broader earnings expectations, compounding the bearish tone set by a sharp European market selloff driven by escalating French debt worries and surging bond yields.

This broader weakness in tech sentiment presents a critical headwind for structural mega-deals; as Eamonn Sheridan at investingLive.com recently highlighted, Elon Musk is reportedly rushing to seal a record $3.7 trillion SpaceX-Tesla merger, a transaction heavily reliant on sustaining market enthusiasm as deal currency.

Despite the macro overhang, Eamonn also noted that Tesla's latest earnings call laid out an aggressive target of 5 million vehicles annually by 2030 alongside a sold-out Megapack supply for 2027.

Meanwhile, other tech giants are engineering corporate pivots to maintain investor confidence, with Meta announcing an effective 2-for-1 stock split via non-voting shares to offset a $9.9 billion legal charge, keeping order flow focused on capital allocation as the earnings season rolls on.

Meta and Tesla: When initial optimism turns into selling

Wednesday, October 21, had been a strong session for Wall Street. The Nasdaq Composite advanced approximately 1.1%, supported by renewed enthusiasm for technology and AI-related companies.

That made the subsequent earnings reactions particularly interesting.

Meta Platforms (META): From a 4% rally to negative territory

Meta initially jumped more than 4% in after-hours trading following its earnings announcement.

There were legitimate reasons for the early optimism. Third-quarter revenue increased 26% year over year to $64.6 billion, supported by advertising growth and progress in its AI initiatives.

However, investors also had to digest the cost of that growth.

Meta reported negative free cash flow of approximately $2.12 billion for the quarter and projected 2026 capital expenditure of $135 billion to $145 billion. The company also announced plans for a new class of non-voting shares to support its investment ambitions.

By Thursday morning, the initial rally had reversed. Meta was down approximately 1.9% in a Reuters premarket update published at 5:40 a.m. Eastern Time.

The question for investors is increasingly whether Meta's AI investments can deliver sufficient future returns to justify their considerable cost.

Tesla (TSLA): A positive earnings reaction that also failed

Tesla offered another example.

Its shares initially gained around 2% after the company released third-quarter results. Positive free cash flow of approximately $1.53 billion, improving gross margins and adjusted earnings that exceeded expectations provided some encouragement.

But that enthusiasm faded as investors evaluated the wider financial picture and management's outlook.

Tesla reduced its 2026 capital expenditure forecast to around $20 billion, compared with its previous expectation of more than $25 billion. The change raised questions about the pace of its ambitious expansion into AI, robotics and autonomous driving.

Tesla shares subsequently reversed lower, falling approximately 5.3% in the same early Thursday premarket Reuters update.

The important observation is the reversal itself.

Investors initially responded positively to aspects of both earnings reports. Later, the market appeared less willing to reward those positives without greater confidence in future profitability and cash generation.

These are premarket observations, not completed Thursday regular-session returns. Nevertheless, they provide a reason to monitor what happens when normal trading resumes.

Netflix had already provided a warning

Earlier in the week, Netflix (NFLX) offered another example of why an earnings beat does not guarantee a positive stock reaction.

Netflix reported third-quarter revenue of approximately $12.87 billion and earnings per share of $0.87, but its outlook disappointed investors.

The company reduced its full-year advertising revenue expectation from approximately $3 billion to $2.7 billion, citing a slower-than-expected rollout of some advertising capabilities.

Its shares subsequently declined.

The three companies face different business challenges. Netflix's concerns relate partly to advertising growth, Tesla's to profitability and investment priorities, and Meta's to the financing and eventual returns from enormous AI spending.

But they share an important characteristic: the market's response was less favorable than some of the reported results might initially have suggested.

That does not mean all three businesses are fundamentally deteriorating. It means investors are becoming more demanding about the relationship between current performance, future expectations and valuations.

Five earnings-season warning signs worth understanding

Investors often concentrate on whether a company beats or misses Wall Street's earnings estimates.

That is useful, but it is only part of the story.

Here are five additional developments that can provide clues about the market's willingness to take risk.

1. Good results, disappointing stock reaction

A company can beat earnings estimates and still experience a substantial share-price decline.

This can happen because investors expected an even better outcome, future guidance disappointed or the stock's valuation already reflected considerable optimism.

The lesson: A company beating expectations is not the same as its stock exceeding investors' expectations.

2. Watch the reaction to the reaction

This is particularly relevant to Meta and Tesla.

The first move following earnings often reflects an immediate interpretation of the headlines. Investors then absorb more detail, including conference-call commentary, expenditure plans and forward guidance.

When an initial rally reverses, it may indicate that buyers are becoming less willing to support the original optimistic interpretation.

However, after-hours trading can involve lower liquidity and sharper price swings. A reversal becomes more meaningful when confirmed during subsequent regular trading sessions.

3. Similar behavior across several major companies

One disappointing earnings reaction could be explained by company-specific problems.

When several influential companies show similar behavior within a short period, the possibility of a broader change in investor sentiment becomes more relevant.

Netflix, Meta and Tesla do not constitute proof of a market-wide problem. They do provide three prominent cases worth comparing with upcoming earnings announcements.

4. Weakness concentrated in the largest stocks

Market capitalization refers to a company's stock market value.

Major indices such as the S&P 500 and Nasdaq-100 are heavily influenced by large companies. A decline in several major constituents can therefore outweigh gains in numerous smaller companies.

This distinction matters for investors holding index funds.

A market may appear relatively balanced when counting how many stocks are rising and falling, yet still suffer meaningful index pressure if the largest companies are doing poorly.

5. Earnings disappointments producing unusually large declines

Options markets can provide an estimate of how far traders expect a stock to move around an earnings announcement.

This is commonly called the implied move. It indicates an anticipated movement range, not a guaranteed limit.

If increasingly large numbers of stocks fall beyond their expected downside ranges, that may suggest a market responding especially harshly to disappointment.

In the provisional October 22 observations underlying this analysis, neither Meta nor Tesla had breached its respective downside expected range. Their significance lies primarily in the failed initial rallies and their influence as major companies, not in exceptionally large individual declines.

Is Wall Street becoming less tolerant of risk?

There is some evidence of increasing selectivity, although it is too early to declare a broader bearish earnings environment.

In the October 13-16 observations considered for this analysis, three of four earnings-reaction sessions showed negative performance when weighted by company size. Downside moves beyond expected ranges also outnumbered upside breaches by 11 to six.

An additional provisional October 22 snapshot showed approximately -2.02% market-capitalization-weighted performance, compared with -0.32% on an equal-weight basis.

Meta and Tesla represented approximately 51.8% of the usable market-capitalization-weighted sample.

These are limited earnings-cohort observations, not returns for the overall stock market, and the sample should not be treated as representative of all reporting companies.

Still, they raise an interesting question: Are earnings-related losses becoming more concentrated in the companies that matter most for the major indices?

There are several possible explanations for the broader unease.

Investors may be reassessing expensive valuations, worrying about the financial burden of AI investment or placing greater emphasis on future cash generation rather than historical earnings beats.

There are also pressures unrelated to individual earnings reports. Rising oil prices, geopolitical uncertainty and broader financial-market volatility weighed on global risk sentiment on Thursday.

It would therefore be a mistake to attribute every price decline solely to a company's results.

What would confirm or weaken the warning?

A single overnight reversal is not sufficient evidence of a sustained market decline.

The next observations are more important than the initial warning.

What would strengthen concerns?

If Meta and Tesla remain weak during regular trading, additional major companies fail to sustain positive earnings reactions, and selling spreads into other sectors, the case for a broader deterioration in sentiment would become more convincing.

Repeated downside moves beyond options-implied expectations would add to those concerns.

What would weaken concerns?

If Meta and Tesla recover their losses, demonstrate sustained buying interest and are joined by positive reactions across a broader range of companies, the initial weakness may prove to have been temporary or company-specific.

Stronger earnings reactions in other industries would be particularly useful evidence that investors remain willing to reward good news.

Investors should distinguish a temporary bout of volatility from a more persistent change in market behavior.

Microsoft, Alphabet and Amazon provide the next important test

The next major technology earnings announcements could offer valuable confirmation or contradiction.

Microsoft (MSFT) and Alphabet (GOOGL/GOOG) are scheduled to report on Wednesday, October 28, while Amazon (AMZN) is scheduled to discuss its third-quarter results on Thursday, October 29.

These companies will give investors additional opportunities to evaluate cloud growth, AI-related expenditures, margins, profitability and management guidance.

The crucial question will not be whether every company beats earnings estimates.

Bulls that bought the initial rally at META right after its after-market-close earnings are especially disappointed and trapped now (if they are still in). Let's look at the 1h chart

Meta's post-earnings rally reverses as sellers take control

Meta Platforms (NASDAQ: META) has experienced a sharp post-earnings reversal. Shares initially surged nearly 8% to just below $749 in after-hours trading, before falling to approximately $676 in premarket trading, almost 10% below that high.

What makes this particularly interesting is the reaction to the initial reaction.

The early rally suggested enthusiasm following earnings, but buyers failed to sustain the advance. Instead, price reversed sharply, breaking below the $705-$711 consolidation area and the pre-earnings closing region around $694-$698.

Two key areas to watch:

  • $673-$675: Immediate support. A sustained break below this area would reinforce the bearish picture, while stabilization could encourage a recovery attempt.

  • $694-$698: The first meaningful recovery test. Reclaiming this area and holding it on a retest would suggest improving buyer interest, with $705-$711 presenting the next obstacle.

The key takeaway is that the reaction after an earnings rally can be more revealing than the initial move. Meta's failed advance suggests that sellers have gained control, at least in the short term.

The next test is whether buyers can defend the recent lows or whether selling pressure continues when regular trading resumes.

NASDAQ: META | One-hour chart | October 22, 2026, premarket snapshot.

It will be whether investors are willing to support positive earnings developments after they have had time to digest the full financial picture.

If encouraging results are repeatedly followed by failed rallies, concerns about investors' appetite for risk would deserve greater attention.

Conversely, sustained positive reactions from these influential companies could suggest that the recent disappointments were selective rather than evidence of a more widespread problem.

The takeaway for stock investors

An earnings report tells us how a business performed relative to expectations.

The subsequent stock reaction tells us something different: whether those results, together with the company's outlook, were enough to justify its existing share price.

The Meta and Tesla reversals make that distinction especially relevant this week.

The market has not established a definitive bearish trend simply because several popular stocks disappointed investors. But the willingness of buyers to defend positive earnings reactions is becoming an increasingly useful development to monitor.

Sometimes the early warning is not the disappointing earnings report. It is the market's inability to hold a rally when the news initially looked encouraging.

item.title: Canada September PPI +2.0% m/m vs +1.3% prior
item.description:
• Prior was +1.3% m/m
  • PPI y/y 14.5% vs 13.5% prior
  • Raw materials price index 4.8% m/m vs 3.3% prior
  • Raw materials price index 27.0% y/y vs 22.9% prior

The market is pricing in an 80% chance of a Bank of Canada rate hike on October 28. This week's CPI number was on the low side but this data point highlights the inflation in the pipeline.

USD/CAD is down 10 pips to 1.4035 today and that highlights how the dynamic in the FX market has totally flipped. S&P 500 futures are down 0.9% but the market sees it as money fleeing the US AI trade, not a traditional 'risk off'.

For background, Canada’s producer price data come in two monthly reports from Statistics Canada: the Industrial Product Price Index (IPPI) and the Raw Materials Price Index (RMPI). They’re typically released together at 8:30 am ET, a few weeks after the reference month ends.

The IPPI measures prices that Canadian manufacturers receive for goods as they leave the factory gate, covering everything from refined petroleum and lumber to metals, chemicals, food products and motor vehicles. The RMPI tracks the prices manufacturers pay for raw materials, including crude oil, metal ores, logs, grains and livestock. Many of those inputs aren’t produced in Canada, so the RMPI is effectively a gauge of global commodity costs flowing into Canadian industry.

The headline figures are the monthly and annual changes in each index, and neither is seasonally adjusted. Because energy dominates, StatCan also publishes the IPPI excluding energy and petroleum products, which gives a cleaner read on broader factory-gate pricing.

The Canadian dollar is a big driver. Many Canadian exports, such as lumber, metals and energy, are priced in US dollars, so a weaker loonie raises the Canadian-dollar value of those goods and lifts the IPPI. A stronger loonie does the opposite. Some swings in the index reflect currency moves rather than any change in underlying pricing pressure.

Unlike the US PPI, the Canadian reports cover only goods and don’t feed into a preferred inflation gauge, so they rarely move markets. They’re mainly watched as an early signal of cost pressures that could eventually reach consumer prices, and of how commodity swings and tariffs are hitting Canadian producers’ margins.

This article was written by Adam Button at investinglive.com.

Details from the release:

  • Initial claims four-week average: 197,750, down 1,000. Prior revised to 198,750 from 198,500.

  • Continuing claims: 1,728,000 vs 1,720,000 est., up 25,000 for the week ending October 10. Prior revised to 1,703,000 from 1,710,000.

  • Continuing claims four-week average: 1,711,000, up 4,000. Prior revised to 1,707,000 from 1,708,750.

  • Insured unemployment rate: 1.1%, unchanged.

US initial jobless claims fell to 194,000, according to the Department of Labor’s weekly report. The decline reverses the previous week’s increase, while the four-week average moved lower as well. Both point to employers continuing to hold on to workers.

The offset came from continuing claims, which increased 25,000 to 1.728 million. That suggests some difficulty finding another job among workers receiving benefits, although one weekly increase does not establish a trend.

Before seasonal adjustment, initial claims fell 19,321, a larger decline than the 14,179 anticipated by seasonal factors. Unadjusted initial and continuing claims also remained below their comparable year-earlier levels.

Quick analysis: Fewer new claims are encouraging, but the hiring side still bears watching. This report gives the Fed little evidence of a sharp deterioration in employment. In isolation, the lower initial reading could support the dollar and Treasury yields by reducing the urgency for rate cuts. The increase in continuing claims tempers that signal. The question now is whether that increase persists.

What this report measures: Initial claims count new applications for unemployment insurance and provide a timely indication of layoffs. Continuing claims track ongoing benefit claims and can help show how quickly unemployed workers are finding jobs. The headline figures are seasonally adjusted, subject to revision, and cover different weeks, with continuing claims lagging initial claims by one week.

item.title: Morning Kickstart: Stocks fall as oil rises on Iran risks
item.description:
Morning Kickstart

Stocks are pointing to a sharply lower opening, crude oil is higher and Treasury yields are moving lower as traders prepare for the North American session. Renewed concerns about military action against Iran are keeping energy risks elevated, while corporate earnings are producing mixed results—and some unforgiving share-price reactions.

The dollar is mixed. The yen and Swiss franc are advancing against the greenback, while the euro, pound, Australian dollar and New Zealand dollar are lower. The Canadian dollar is holding a modest gain as crude oil moves back toward $100.

In the morning video above, I take a look at the three major currency pairs—EURUSD, USDJPY and GBPUSD—from a technical perspective. For each pair, I outline the bias, the risk-defining levels and the targets that would give either the buyers or sellers more control.

Middle East: Strike concerns return to the forefront

The overnight news has shifted attention back toward the possibility of renewed military escalation. InvestingLive’s Asia-Pacific coverage highlighted reports of US and Israeli preparations for further strikes on Iran. Separate coverage cited a New York Times report that military planners had prepared options for a short, intense round of strikes after the US midterm elections. Preparations do not establish that an operation has been approved, but they keep the threat in focus. investinglive.com

Adding to that concern, an Al Arabiya headline reported that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu would inform President Trump of Israel’s intentions but would not seek his permission to strike Iran.

For markets, the uncertainty remains the problem. Hopes for a diplomatic breakthrough have repeatedly competed with threats of further attacks. Traders are left weighing what another escalation could mean for regional energy supplies and shipping.

InvestingLive’s overnight coverage captures that shift: Oil rises as hopes for a deal fade amid growing prospects of another US attack on Iran. investinglive.com

Crude oil moves back toward $100

Crude oil is trading at $99.25, up $2.08 or 2.12%.

The rise puts the $100 level back within reach and keeps energy costs in the inflation discussion. It also adds another concern for equity traders already digesting a busy earnings calendar.

The headline risk remains two-sided. Concrete diplomatic progress could remove some of the geopolitical premium, while further escalation could add to it. That makes following the price action—and defining risk against the technical levels—particularly important.

US stock futures point to a sharply lower opening

The major US stock-index futures are lower:

  • Dow futures: Down 317 points.
  • S&P 500 futures: Down 76 points.
  • Nasdaq futures: Down 500 points.

The earnings reactions show that beating the published estimates is only part of the story. Traders also judge guidance, the quality of the results and how much good news was already priced into the shares. The geopolitical tension is also another reason for the reversal for some of them.  

Meta, IBM and Lam Research are examples this morning. Each delivered beats on the measures outlined below, but their shares are lower.

Earnings released after yesterday’s close

EPS excluding the charge would have been $7.40—$3.83 reported plus the $3.57 charge—versus $6.67 expected. Reported EPS of $3.83 missed that estimate. Revenue of $64.6 billion topped $63.31 billion expected. Shares are down 2.65% this morning.

Full-year adjusted operating profit guidance of €11.8–€12.2 billion exceeded €11.7 billion expected. Shares are up 0.38%. The profit measure here is operating profit rather than EPS.

  • Tesla (TSLA): Adjusted EPS BEAT; revenue MISSED. Adjusted EPS of $0.48 exceeded $0.45 expected, but revenue of $28.0 billion fell short of $28.1 billion expected. The after-hours share reaction provided was up 3.46%.

Earnings released this morning

Fourth-quarter operating income guidance of €820 million, however, exceeded €813.4 million expected. Shares are up 4.88%, with the stronger profit outlook helping the reaction.

The dollar is mixed, with the yen outperforming

The decline in US yields is consistent with the pressure on USDJPY. For currency traders, the next question is whether the price can sustain its move through the relevant technical levels or whether buyers begin to lean against support.

Gold, silver and Bitcoin move lower

North American calendar: Jobless claims lead the way

The calendar provides several checkpoints, although earnings and Middle East headlines could continue to dominate. All times below are ET.

  • 8:30 AM — US initial jobless claims:200,000 expected, versus 199,000 previously. The prior four-week average was 198,500.

Jobless claims will provide the first scheduled check on labor-market conditions. A reading close to expectations would suggest layoffs remain contained, while a meaningful surprise could give yields and currencies another reason to move.

For traders, the task is to let the news develop while using the technical levels to judge the reaction. Does a break attract follow-through? Can the price stay beyond the level? That is what would give buyers or sellers more control.

item.title: Market playbook: Why a convincing market story doesn't always make a good trade
item.description:
If you've been in markets long enough, I'll bet you have surely encountered a situation where you were absolutely sure that something was going to happen. And as it turned out, you called it and you were right. But somehow, you still ended up losing money on the trade. Does that sound familiar?

Well, I would say it's one of the biggest traps that a trader can fall into. It is the very fact that even having a convincing market story doesn't necessarily mean you have a good trade.

Let's go back to our little apple store example, shall we?

Just imagine that you are selling apples and one day, you hear that bad weather has damaged apple harvests across the country. With that information, you quickly make the connection that supplies are going to fall and apple prices should go up because of that.

Hence, you decide to stock up on apples at $2 each, hoping to sell them for $3 later. That sounds like a decent business opportunity, no?

But then, here's the catch though. You're not the only person with this information. Everyone else has heard about the bad weather too and other sellers have already rushed to buy apples, pushing the price from $1 to $2 before you even had a chance to get in on the action.

And by the time you do and when the shortage does hit, apple prices only go up from $2 to $2.05. You were right about the shortage. You were even right that prices did go higher. But after accounting for transport, storage and other expenses, you might have barely made any money on the sale - if at all.

Now, there's even a worse scenario than that. What if the bad weather did not do as much damage on apple harvests as initially anticipated? Apple prices could fall back quickly to $1.70, , leaving you with a loss despite having a perfectly reasonable argument.

It's the same thing as trading and in markets too.

Let's say that you anticipate inflation will rise because oil prices are surging higher to above $100 again. You make the connection that higher oil prices can push up consumer prices more broadly at some point, potentially forcing central banks to keep interest rates higher for longer.

So, you take action in buying the dollar as you expect the Fed to keep tighter monetary policy compared to other central banks, which should give the dollar some support. But then, here's the catch again. What if everyone else has already made that same trade?

The dollar might have rallied considerably before you even got involved. And when inflation eventually comes in higher, the currency might barely react because markets had already anticipated it. Worse still, you might even be hit with a case of buy the rumour, sell the fact. And that's a painful lesson to learn as you would have lost money on the trade despite getting the economic story right.

As such, it is always important as a trader to pose the question of what markets have already priced in and how much further could prices realistically move. But perhaps also more importantly, you need to understand and grasp how much you stand to lose if you're wrong.

Because knowing that apples will become more expensive is one thing, but knowing whether they're still worth buying at today's price is another. And in trading, that difference itself can cost you money.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.

item.title: Why following crypto ETF flows is like looking in the rear-view mirror
item.description:
Crypto ETF flows have become a popular indicator for gauging institutional demand. Strong inflows are often interpreted as bullish, while sustained outflows are seen as a warning sign. However, ETF flows tell you what investors have already done, not what they are likely to do next.

By the time large inflows appear in the data, prices may have already rallied on the news that attracted investors. Similarly, outflows often accelerate after a selloff has begun. Traders who rely solely on these figures risk buying near the top or selling near the bottom, becoming the bagholders of a move that has already played out.

Instead of waiting for ETF data to confirm a trend, traders should focus on what could trigger the next change in demand. For example, a softer than expected US inflation report could lead markets to price in a more dovish Federal Reserve, lower yields and easier financial conditions. This could encourage investors to increase their crypto allocations. Rather than waiting for ETF inflows to appear in the data, traders can immediately start to position for the expected increase. 

The same goes for ETF outflows. Rising geopolitical tensions, persistent inflation or deteriorating growth can weigh on risk sentiment and outflows as investors reduce risk. Focusing on what actually drives ETF flows allows a trader to anticipate changes in investor behaviour.

Of course, the relationship is not always straightforward. Weak economic data might encourage rate cut expectations but also increase recession fears, in which case the negative risk sentiment is likely to weigh on the crypto market and lead to ETF outflows. The key is to focus on catalysts that can trigger changes in investors' sentiment. Generally speaking, cryptocurrencies are just another risk asset, so they respond to changes in risk sentiment much like the stock market. 

ETF inflows do not guarantee further upside. If investors have already priced in a favourable outlook, additional buying may weaken even while the latest flow figures remain positive. Traders who enter solely because inflows are increasing could end up buying just as the rally runs out of steam.

Likewise, heavy outflows do not automatically mean prices will continue falling. If the catalyst behind the selling begins to fade, the market could recover before the flow data turns positive. This is why ETF flows are a lagging indicator.

This article was written by Giuseppe Dellamotta at investinglive.com.

item.title: EUR/CHF falls to three-month lows as French bond turmoil raises fresh euro risks
item.description:
It might not seem like it, but the euro is finding itself in a rather uncomfortable spot in trading today. While EUR/USD is holding up relatively better amid the broader market turmoil, EUR/CHF is perhaps telling us a more worrying story about the risks building in Europe.

The latest drop today sees the pair briefly touch its lowest level in three months, slipping to 0.9220 levels now as the Swiss franc draws renewed support from its traditional safe-haven appeal. But what is driving that?

Well, it's the thing we have been talking about every so often in the past two weeks, that being France's fiscal plight. And the worries are now growing rather quickly as French 10-year government bond yields have surged above 5%, hitting their highest levels since 2002.

Besides that, the France-Germany 10-year yield spread is now widening towards a staggering 170 bps - its highest since 2011. It wasn't just too long ago that we were talking the line in the sand at 150 bps. All of a sudden, we're now nearly 20 bps up from that. The latest surge is another sign that investors are demanding a much higher premium to hold French debt, amid growing fiscal and political uncertainty.

Looking at the EUR/CHF chart, we're already seeing some of those worries translate into price action. After all, France is Europe's second-largest economy and concerns there will have the potential to spill over into broader European assets and the euro.

The pair has already broken below its trendline support from the March to May lows, before surrendering the key 0.9300 level as the 100-day moving average (red line) also gave way. And the latest decline is now also challenging to break the 200-day moving average (blue line) around 0.9235.

A sustained break below that could invite a deeper push towards 0.9200 initially, before the June to July lows may offer a bit of support around 0.9180. Beyond that, the next notable downside level sits closer to 0.9100.

As for the Swiss franc side of the equation, let's not forget that the SNB had only recently toned down its language on foreign exchange intervention. The central bank hinted at less urgency to push back against franc strength. But with European risks now escalating and EUR/CHF threatening a more meaningful technical breakdown, I wonder if policymakers might soon have to reconsider that stance.

For now though, the EUR/CHF chart is certainly not giving the euro much reason for comfort as it arguably best captures the risks surrounding European bond markets.

item.title: US futures tumble as AI rally faces fresh scrutiny despite solid Meta earnings
item.description:
US futures are taking quite a beating today as what looked to be a promising rebound in Wall Street yesterday is already threatening to unravel. S&P 500 futures are down 1% with Nasdaq futures down 1.7% as tech shares are bearing the brunt of the selling.

Tensions in the Middle East are once again pushing up oil prices, so that is arguably keeping investors on edge. But then, you have Treasury yields falling as 10-year yields are down to 5.08% today. Ordinarily, that should offer some relief to tech shares amid their lofty valuations. But not today, it seems.

In any case, I would argue that the bigger problem lies with earnings and whether the AI rally can continue to live up to the enormous expectations already priced in.

Now, Meta's earnings did at least offer some encouragement with revenue jumping 26% to $64.6 billion and its shares holding up relatively well. Shares are trading about 0.8% higher in after-hours trading but that optimism isn't translating into broader confidence across the tech sector.

Just look at Lam Research. The semiconductor equipment maker reported record quarterly revenue of around $8.2 billion, beating estimates, yet its shares have tumbled by over 8% in after-hours trading. Even a strong quarter wasn't enough as investors chose to focus on the weaker-than-expected forward earnings forecast instead.

Besides that, there's also Tesla getting into trouble after its own earnings release with shares down roughly 5% in after-hours trading. Meanwhile, smaller semiconductor firm NVE Corporation is seeing its shares sink by over 22% after reporting an 8% decline in quarterly revenue.

These are rather different earnings stories but collectively, they paint a picture of a market that is becoming much less forgiving. Much, much less.

And I think the bond market is also telling us something here. With Treasury yields falling even as oil prices rise, could investors be starting to worry more about US economic growth than inflation?

You might think that if yields are easing, it would help provide some comfort for stocks. However, that sort of relationship is not exactly straighforward. If yields are falling because investors are becoming nervous about the economic outlook, then the implications for corporate earnings and the stock market outlook are hardly encouraging as well.

For the AI trade, the latest market mood simply reinforces the narrative that investor expectations are becoming much harder to justify especially when the economy starts losing momentum. In particular, companies with heavy borrowing finance their AI ambitions are arguably the ones that will be hit the hardest.

Now, I wouldn't call this the end of the AI rally just yet. But when record earnings and falling Treasury yields can't provide much support to equities, it may be a case that Wall Street is finally starting to question whether the bar has been set too high. And waking up to that very reality could end up being extremely painful.

This article was written by Justin Low at investinglive.com.
